meaning: “Regardless of ...” There are several possibilities, but none of them affects the result.
connection: Noun + にかかわらず; verb affirmative + negative + にかかわらず

senses.label: Regardless of (noun)
senses.meaning: The first part is a noun that covers several cases, such as 「天候」, 「年齢」, or 「性別」. Whatever the case, the result is the same. The result is a neutral decision or rule, without dissatisfaction or surprise.
senses.connection: Noun + にかかわらず (often 「天候」, 「年齢」, 「経験の有無」, 「結果」, etc.)
examples: Anyone can join, regardless of age.
The game will go ahead as planned, regardless of the weather.
We welcome motivated people, with or without experience.

senses.label: Whether or not
senses.meaning: Puts the affirmative and negative side by side: “whether you do or not”. Neither case affects the result.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + verb nai-form + にかかわらず; 〜か〜ないか + にかかわらず; opposites like 好き嫌い or 大小 + にかかわらず
examples: Please reply whether or not you'll be attending.
Like them or not, eat your vegetables too.

senses.label: にかかわりなく
senses.meaning: Means the same as 「にかかわらず」 in a slightly different form. Equally formal; common in rules and notices.
senses.connection: Noun + にかかわりなく
examples: Anyone may apply, regardless of nationality.

notes: The kanji can be 「に関わらず」 or 「に拘わらず」 with the same meaning. Official documents usually use hiragana or 「関わらず」.
Don't confuse it with 「にもかかわらず」 (despite). That one extra 「も」 changes the meaning completely.
In speech, 「〜に関係なく」 is more common; 「〜を問わず」 is more formal.

daily.title: A community event notice
daily.description: A neighborhood notice says the event goes ahead even if it rains.
daily.example: The festival will be held rain or shine.

daily.title: Free shipping info from an online shop
daily.description: A shopping site says all orders are treated the same.
daily.example: Shipping is free regardless of how much you buy.

daily.title: A gym advertisement
daily.description: A gym appeals to members of all ages.
daily.example: Exercise is good for you, whatever your age.

work.title: A job ad
work.description: A company says no experience is required.
work.example: We welcome applications whether or not you have experience.

work.title: An RSVP for an invitation
work.description: Organizers ask everyone to reply about attendance.
work.example: Please let us know by the end of this week whether or not you will attend.

etymology: Formed from 「かかわら」, the irrealis form of the verb 「かかわる」 (関わる／係わる／拘わる, "to be involved in, to concern, to be bound by"), plus the continuative form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」. Literally "not being involved with ..., not being bound by ...", it became grammaticalized as "regardless of ...". Since 「ず」 is a classical negative, the pattern has a written, formal feel. In modern Japanese both spellings 「拘わらず」 and 「関わらず」 exist side by side; the standard spelling in the Joyo kanji list is 「関わる」.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: With an extra 「も」, the meaning is completely different: it expresses contrast, "despite ..., still ...", where the result goes against expectations, with a tone of surprise or dissatisfaction. 「雨にかかわらず行く」 = I'll go whether it rains or not (the condition doesn't matter); 「雨にもかかわらず行った」 = I went despite the rain (contrast with a fact).

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning as にかかわらず (regardless of), but more written and common in job ads: 「年齢・性別を問わず」. It usually follows pairs of opposite nouns like 男女, 昼夜, 国内外, and generally not affirmative-negative verb pairs.

similar.title: 〜に関係なく
similar.explanation: Same meaning but more colloquial and direct: 「天気に関係なく行きます」. In everyday conversation it is more common than にかかわらず.

meaning: “Despite ...”, “even though ...” The first part is an established fact, but the result goes against expectations.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem (+ である) + にもかかわらず; verb / i-adjective plain form + にもかかわらず

senses.label: Despite
senses.meaning: The first part is something that has actually happened, not a hypothesis. The second part is an unexpected result. It often carries surprise, astonishment, or dissatisfaction.
senses.connection: Noun (+ である) / verb / i-adjective plain form + にもかかわらず
examples: Despite the rain, a big crowd gathered.
Even though he had a fever, he came to work.
Despite trying my hardest, I didn't pass.

senses.label: Despite being busy (thanks)
senses.meaning: Used in formal thanks: “even though you are busy (or it's inconvenient), you did this for us”. A set phrase in business and ceremonies.
senses.connection: お忙しい／ご多忙 + にもかかわらず + 〜いただき、ありがとうございます
examples: Thank you for attending despite your busy schedule.
Thank you for coming despite the bad weather.

senses.label: As a conjunction
senses.meaning: On its own at the start of a sentence, it links to the previous one, like 「それなのに」: “nevertheless”. Formal and objective in tone.
senses.connection: (それ)にもかかわらず、〜
examples: I warned him many times. Nevertheless, he made the same mistake again.

notes: The second part states a fact. It can't be a command, request, or intention (not ×雨にもかかわらず来てください).
The kanji can be 「にも関わらず」 or 「にも拘わらず」. It sounds more formal and objective than 「のに」.

daily.title: Complaining that a friend stood you up
daily.description: Telling someone a friend promised to come but didn't.
daily.example: Even though he promised, he didn't come.

daily.title: Talking about a game
daily.description: Reacting to a team's performance after watching.
daily.example: Despite being in a tough spot, the team came from behind to win.

work.title: Thanks at the start of a meeting
work.description: The host thanks attendees for coming despite busy schedules.
work.example: Thank you all for gathering here today despite your busy schedules.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting on a bill passed despite opposition.
work.example: Despite strong opposition, the bill was passed.

etymology: The structure is case particle 「に」 + particle 「も」 + 「かかわらず」. 「かかわらず」 comes from the irrealis form of the verb 「かかわる」 (関わる／拘わる) plus the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」, meaning "not being constrained by ...". With 「も」 added, it literally means "even in such a situation, not being affected by it", which developed into the contrastive "despite ..., still ...". It shares its origin with 「にかかわらず」, but because of the emphatic 「も」, the meaning shifted from "the condition doesn't matter" to "contrast with an actual fact".

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Also contrastive, but のに is very colloquial and more emotional (dissatisfaction, regret), and the second part can be left unsaid at the end of a sentence: 「せっかく作ったのに…」. にもかかわらず is more written and objective, and the second part must be stated.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: Without 「も」 it means "regardless of ...": the first part is a range of possible conditions unrelated to the result. With にもかかわらず, the first part is a single established fact and the second part contradicts it.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Also expresses contrast, "although ..., ...", but ものの focuses on "the first part is true, but things didn't develop as expected", often about one's own actions (買ったものの使わない); it is weaker than にもかかわらず, with less surprise or reproach.

meaning: “There's no way ...”, “can't possibly ...” Strongly denies a possibility based on logic or common sense.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + わけがない; na-adjective stem + な / noun + の + わけがない

senses.label: No way
senses.meaning: The speaker judges, by logic or common sense, that something is completely impossible. The tone is subjective and firm, much stronger than 「〜ないだろう」.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + わけがない／わけはない; noun + の / na-adjective + な + わけがない
examples: There's no way a child could solve a problem this hard.
Someone as honest as him would never lie.
At this price, there's no way it's the real thing.

senses.label: Casual / pushing back
senses.meaning: In speech, 「が」 is often dropped: 「わけない」. With 「でしょう／だろ」 at the end, it sounds like you're pushing back or getting impatient.
senses.connection: 〜わけない(だろ／でしょ); rough: 「〜わけねえ」
examples: We practiced so much. There's no way we'll lose.
How on earth would I know something like that?

notes: The polite form is 「わけがありません」. In kanji it's 「訳がない」, but hiragana is more common in writing.
「わけではない」 is a partial denial (it's not that ...), and 「わけにはいかない」 means you can't in good conscience. Both are different from this.
「申し訳ない」 is a set phrase unrelated to this grammar point.

daily.title: Denying a friend's suspicion
daily.description: A friend thinks you ate the cake, and you deny it right away.
daily.example: As if I'd eat it!

daily.title: Psyching yourself up before a game
daily.description: Encouraging your teammates before a match.
daily.example: We've practiced every day. There's no way we'll lose.

daily.title: Spotting a fake
daily.description: Seeing a designer bag online at a ridiculously low price.
daily.example: There's no way it's genuine at this price.

work.title: Defending a coworker
work.description: Someone suspects a coworker made an error, and you think it's impossible.
work.example: There's no way Tanaka-san would make a mistake like that.

etymology: 「わけ」 is written 「訳」 and originally meant "logic, reason, cause of things" (cognate with the verb 「分ける」, "the logic one has discerned"). 「わけがない」 literally means "there's no (such) reason", and by extension "by all logic it's impossible". The kanji 「訳」 was borrowed later to write the word; its meaning "translate" has nothing to do with this.

similar.title: 〜はずがない
similar.explanation: Also means "impossible", and the two are mostly interchangeable. はずがない leans toward inference based on specific grounds or plans (I definitely locked it, so it can't have been stolen); わけがない leans toward impossibility by common sense and reasoning, and sounds more subjective and stronger.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: The affirmative わけだ means "no wonder, naturally ...", a conclusion drawn from facts; わけがない denies a possibility. They point in opposite directions.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Expresses partial negation, "it's not that ...": 「嫌いなわけではない」 = it's not that I dislike it. わけがない completely denies a possibility; don't confuse them.

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Means "can't do" because of social norms or moral obligation, as in 「休むわけにはいかない」; it has nothing to do with judging possibility.

meaning: “Have no choice but to ...” Circumstances force you to do or conclude something, even if you'd rather not.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ざるを得ない; する → せざるを得ない

senses.label: Forced to do
senses.meaning: Circumstances or pressure leave you no other option, so you have to do it. It carries a sense of reluctance. It feels more forced than 「しなければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form minus ない + ざるを得ない (する→せざる, 来る→こざる)
examples: It's an order from my boss, so I have no choice but to obey.
With a typhoon approaching, the game had to be canceled.

senses.label: Must admit / have to say
senses.meaning: Used with verbs of thinking or speaking like 「認める」, 「言う」, and 「思う」. Based on the facts, you can't avoid this conclusion. Common in commentary and reports.
senses.connection: 認め／言わ／思わ + ざるを得ない
examples: With this much evidence, I have to admit it.
Unfortunately, I have to say the plan was a failure.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せざるを得ない」. ×しざるを得ない is wrong.
「得ない」 is read 「えない」, and it's often written in hiragana as 「ざるをえない」.
Past: 「ざるを得なかった」; polite: 「ざるを得ません」; written connective: 「ざるを得ず」.

daily.title: Missing the last train
daily.description: Explaining to family why you took a taxi home.
daily.example: I missed the last train, so I had no choice but to take a taxi home.

daily.title: Canceling plans because you're sick
daily.description: Messaging a friend to explain.
daily.example: My fever won't go down, so I have to cancel the trip.

work.title: Announcing a cancellation
work.description: Organizers explain to participants why an event was canceled.
work.example: Due to the typhoon, we were forced to cancel the event.

work.title: Evaluating project results
work.description: Assessing a project objectively at a review meeting.
work.example: Judging by these numbers, I have to say it was a failure.

etymology: 「ざる」 is the attributive form of the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 (the supplementary conjugation of ず — ざら・ざり・ざる・ざれ — came from the fusion of 「ず＋あり」). 「〜ざる」 can act as a noun-like element, followed by the object marker 「を」 and 「得ない」, the negative of 「得る（える）」, the modern form of the verb 「得（う）」 (to be able, to obtain). Literally "cannot manage not to do ..." — a double negative expressing necessity, and a remnant of classical grammar in modern written Japanese.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Expresses obligation or necessity, "must ...", a neutral rule or duty; ざるを得ない stresses "there's no other option, I have to do it against my will", with a sense of resignation and compulsion.

similar.title: 〜ないわけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Also means "can't not do", but the reasons are usually social norms, personal relationships, or morals (you can't not go to a friend's wedding); ざるを得ない is more about being forced by objective circumstances.

similar.title: 〜しかない／〜ほかない
similar.explanation: "Can only ...", meaning there's no other way; more colloquial and calmer in tone. ざるを得ない is more written, with a stronger sense of being forced.

meaning: “Nothing more than ...”, “merely ...” Stresses that the degree, amount, or status is low: “that's all it is”.
connection: Noun + にすぎない; verb / i-adjective plain form + にすぎない

senses.label: Nothing but
senses.meaning: Plays something down: “it's no big deal”. Often with 「ただの」 or 「単なる」 for emphasis. More formal than 「だけだ」, with a dismissive tone.
senses.connection: Noun + にすぎない (often with 「ただの」 or 「単なる」)
examples: That's nothing more than an excuse.
That story turned out to be just a rumor.

senses.label: Only (a small amount)
senses.meaning: After a number, it stresses how small it is. Often with 「わずか」 or 「たった」. Common in news and reports.
senses.connection: (わずか) number + にすぎない／にすぎず
examples: There were only ten participants, and the venue was nearly empty.
Voter turnout was only 30%.

senses.label: Modesty
senses.meaning: Used about yourself to say your position is humble or what you did is trivial. A modest way of speaking.
senses.connection: Noun / verb ta-form + にすぎません
examples: I'm just a regular employee, so I don't have the authority to decide.
I merely passed on his opinion.

notes: In kanji it's 「に過ぎない」; both spellings are common.
The written connective is 「にすぎず」, and the literary form is 「にすぎぬ」. In everyday speech, 「〜だけだ」 is more common.

daily.title: Reassuring a friend about a rumor
daily.description: A friend is worried by gossip, and you tell them not to mind.
daily.example: That's nothing but a rumor.

daily.title: Modestly accepting praise
daily.description: Someone praises you, and you respond humbly.
daily.example: I just happened to get lucky.

work.title: Explaining your authority to a client
work.description: An employee explains they can't decide on the spot.
work.example: I'm just the person handling this, so I'll consult my manager.

work.title: Analyzing data in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out that a figure isn't actually good.
work.example: Respondents make up only 10% of the total.

etymology: Made of the case particle 「に」 + the negative of the verb すぎる (in Classical Japanese the kami-nidan verb すぐ). すぎる originally means "to exceed, to pass", so 「〜にすぎない」 literally means "does not go beyond ... (this degree)", and by extension "is merely ...". In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese, 「〜ニスギズ」 was used to render the Chinese expression for "nothing but ...", and the modern written 「にすぎず」 is a remnant of this form.

similar.title: 〜だけだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (only ...), but だけだ is a neutral limitation common in speech; にすぎない carries an evaluation of "not worth mentioning, low in degree" and is more written.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: "Is precisely ..., is nothing other than ...", an emphatic assertion (成功は努力の結果にほかならない) with no belittling sense; にすぎない evaluates something as low.

similar.title: 〜でしかない
similar.explanation: "Is only ...", very close to にすぎない and also negative in evaluation; slightly more colloquial.

meaning: “Could well ...”, “might end up ...” There's a risk of a bad outcome, with a tone of worry or warning.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + かねない

senses.label: Risk of a bad outcome
senses.meaning: Some bad result could happen. The speaker uses it to warn or caution. Only for negative outcomes; you can't say ×成功しかねない.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + かねない (often with 「このままでは」 or 「下手をすると」)
examples: At this rate, it could lead to a serious accident.
Putting it that way could cause a misunderstanding.
If left alone, it could develop into a major problem.

senses.label: Capable of it
senses.meaning: Judging someone's character or habits: “he's just the type to do something like that”. Negative in tone.
senses.connection: Person + なら + verb masu-stem + かねない
examples: He's the kind of person who might say something that awful.
That person might actually do it.

notes: The polite 「かねません」 still means “might ...”. Don't confuse it with 「かねます」 (can't really ...).
It is more formal than 「かもしれない」 and only for bad things. A more objective option is 「おそれがある」.

daily.title: Telling a friend to slow down
daily.description: Riding in a friend's car and asking them to drive slower.
daily.example: If you drive that fast, you could cause an accident.

daily.title: Urging family to see a doctor
daily.description: A family member has been coughing for days and won't go to the doctor.
daily.example: If you ignore it, it could turn into pneumonia.

work.title: Flagging a wording problem
work.description: After reading a coworker's email to a client, pointing out an issue.
work.example: This wording could be misunderstood, so let's revise it.

work.title: Raising a risk in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out the consequences of delay at a project meeting.
work.example: At this rate, we may well miss the delivery deadline.

etymology: 「かねる」 is written 「兼ねる」, originally meaning "to serve two roles at once, to combine" (大は小を兼ねる, "the large can serve for the small"). It is generally thought that "it's hard to handle two things at once" led to its use as an auxiliary verb after other verbs meaning "find it hard to ..., cannot ..." (→かねる). 「かねない」 is its negative, literally "it's not that it can't", i.e. "it's entirely possible", which then specialized into "something bad may happen". This negative use is thought to have spread from around the early modern period.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: The affirmative かねる means "find it hard to ..., cannot ..." (お答えしかねます). かねない means "might ...", almost the opposite; take special care to distinguish 「かねます」 from 「かねません」.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: A neutral "maybe, possibly", usable for good or bad things; かねない is only for bad outcomes, carries a tone of concern or warning, and is more written.

similar.title: 〜おそれがある
similar.explanation: "There's a danger of ..."; very close to かねない, but more objective and written, common in weather forecasts and news (津波のおそれがある). It attaches as verb dictionary form / noun + の + おそれがある.

meaning: “Can't really ...”, “find it hard to ...” Something is difficult because of your position or feelings. Commonly used as a polite refusal.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + かねる

senses.label: Polite refusal
senses.meaning: A set expression for declining requests in service and business. Softer and more appropriate than 「できません」. Common forms: 「〜いたしかねます」, 「〜しかねます」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + かねます (いたしかねます／応じかねます／お答えしかねます)
examples: I'm very sorry, but we are unable to comment on that matter.
We regret that we are unable to accommodate your request.

senses.label: Hard to accept
senses.meaning: You can't agree with something or bring yourself to do it. Often with 「賛成する」, 「理解する」, or 「決める」.
senses.connection: 賛成し／理解し／決め + かねる
examples: I really can't understand his attitude.
I can't agree with that proposal.

senses.label: Set phrases: 見かねる, 待ちかねる
senses.meaning: 「見るに見かねて」 means “unable to stand by and watch any longer”. 「待ちかねる」 means “to wait impatiently, to have long looked forward to”.
senses.connection: 見るに見かねて; 待ちかねる／待ちかねた
examples: I couldn't just stand by and watch, so I helped him.
The kids can't wait for summer vacation.

notes: The negative 「かねない」 means something completely different (“might ...”). Be careful to tell 「かねます」 from 「かねません」.
It isn't used for lack of ability. If you can't swim, say 「泳げない」, not ×泳ぎかねる.

daily.title: Helping a stranger
daily.description: Seeing an elderly person carrying something heavy up the stairs, you can't help stepping in.
daily.example: I couldn't just stand there, so I carried his bags for him.

daily.title: A clerk declines a return
daily.description: A customer wants to return an opened item, and the clerk politely declines.
daily.example: We're unable to accept returns on opened items.

work.title: Declining in a business email
work.description: Politely turning down a client's request for a discount.
work.example: We truly apologize, but we are unable to offer any further discount.

work.title: Expressing reservations in a meeting
work.description: Not quite agreeing with your boss's proposal.
work.example: At this point, I can't quite agree with that proposal.

etymology: 「かねる」 is written 「兼ねる」, originally meaning "to combine, to have both, to serve in two roles at once" (大は小を兼ねる). It is generally thought that "it's hard to handle two things at once" led to its use as an auxiliary verb after the verb continuative form meaning "find it hard to ..."; this use, as 「〜かぬ」 (the classical shimo-nidan 「かぬ」), is already found in Middle Japanese. As an auxiliary verb today it is usually written in hiragana as 「かねる」.

similar.title: 〜かねない
similar.explanation: The negative かねない means "could well (lead to something bad)". 「お答えしかねます」 = we cannot answer; 「誤解を招きかねません」 = it may cause a misunderstanding.

similar.title: 〜にくい
similar.explanation: "Hard to ...", usually about physical or objective difficulty (読みにくい字); かねる focuses on psychological difficulty or one's position, and is often a polite refusal.

similar.title: 〜できない
similar.explanation: States directly that one cannot or may not; かねる is an indirect refusal and more appropriate in service and business settings.

meaning: “In ...”, “at ...” Marks the place, time, or field in which something happens. A formal version of 「で」.
connection: Noun + において(は／も); before a noun: noun + における + noun

senses.label: Place / time
senses.meaning: The place or time an action or event takes place. Like 「で」, but more formal. Common in notices and ceremony announcements.
senses.connection: Place / time noun + において
examples: The meeting will be held in Conference Room 1.
The entrance ceremony will be held in the gymnasium.

senses.label: Field / area
senses.meaning: The field, area, or era concerned. Often combined with 「は」 or 「も」: 「においては」, 「においても」.
senses.connection: Field noun + において(は／も)
examples: In modern society, information is extremely important.
He also excels in research.

senses.label: における + noun
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「における」: “... in ...”. Common in academic papers and news headlines.
senses.connection: Noun + における + noun
examples: I researched the declining birthrate in Japan.
Population concentration in Tokyo has become a problem.

notes: In everyday speech, 「で」 is normal; 「において」 sounds stiff and formal.
It can be written 「に於いて」, but hiragana is usual today. Don't confuse it with the verb use 「机の上に置いて」 (put it on the desk).

daily.title: A local event poster
daily.description: A community poster gives the venue.
daily.example: The summer festival will be held in Central Park.

daily.title: Reading a news headline
daily.description: A headline you read in the morning news.
daily.example: Aging in rural areas is accelerating.

work.title: Writing a thesis
work.description: Defining the scope of research in a paper.
work.example: In this study, we analyze the consumer behavior of young people.

work.title: A formal meeting notice
work.description: The general affairs department announces the venue.
work.example: The briefing will be held in the third-floor conference room at the head office.

etymology: It comes from the case particle 「に」 + 「おい」, the sound-changed continuative form of the verb 「置く（おく）」 (to place), + the conjunctive particle 「て」, literally "placed at ...". In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese, this form was used to render the Chinese preposition 「於」, so it was written 「に於いて」 and gradually became fixed as a written particle for place, time, and scope. 「における」 is generally thought to come from 「おけ」, the realis form of 「置く」, plus 「る」, the attributive form of the classical perfective/continuative auxiliary 「り」, literally "which is placed at ...", used to modify nouns.

similar.title: 〜で (case particle)
similar.explanation: The most basic way to mark the place or time of an action, used in both speech and writing; において is more formal and written, and can also express abstract fields or scope.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: Means "about ...", marking the topic of talk or thought; において marks the place or field where something occurs, not a topic. 「日本における問題」 (problems that exist in Japan) ≠ 「日本についての問題」 (questions about Japan).

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: "For ..., to ...", marking the standpoint of an evaluation; において marks an occasion or field and cannot express whose standpoint is taken.

meaning: “Although ..., (still) ...” Acknowledges the first part as fact, but things didn't go as expected afterward.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ものの; na-adjective stem + な / noun + である + ものの

senses.label: Although ..., not ...
senses.meaning: The first part is an established fact; the second is something that doesn't match it or falls short. 「〜たものの」 often describes doing something with no follow-through. The tone is calm and formal.
senses.connection: Verb plain form (often ta-form) / i-adjective + ものの
examples: I bought a new camera, but I haven't used it once.
I graduated from university, but I still haven't found a job.
I understand it in my head, but I just can't put it into practice.

senses.label: とはいうものの
senses.meaning: A set form meaning “that said”, “even so”. It can appear mid-sentence or alone at the start of a sentence to follow on from what came before.
senses.connection: Plain form + とはいうものの; at the start: 「とはいうものの、〜」
examples: Although it's officially spring, the cold days keep coming.
That said, it's still not easy.

notes: The second part can't be an intention, command, or request.
Nouns can't attach directly. Say 「学生であるものの」.
It stresses the gap between the two parts more than 「けれども」 or 「が」.

daily.title: An unused gym membership
daily.description: Telling a friend you signed up but never go.
daily.example: I joined a gym, but I've hardly gone.

daily.title: Diet struggles
daily.description: Writing about mixed feelings in your diary.
daily.example: I want to lose weight, but I can't give up sweets.

work.title: An economic report
work.description: Acknowledging something first, then turning in a report.
work.example: Although the economy is recovering, consumer spending remains weak.

work.title: Looking back on job interviews
work.description: Updating a career counselor on your job search.
work.example: I had the interview, but I haven't heard back yet.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「もの」 plus the particle 「の」. In Middle Japanese (Heian period) prose, 「ものの」 was already used as a conjunctive particle expressing contrast ("although ..., still"), frequently seen in waka poetry and tales. Modern Japanese inherited this use, which is why it has a somewhat written, literary feel.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: Also expresses contrast, but のに carries strong dissatisfaction, surprise, or regret and is very colloquial; ものの is calmer, more objective, and written.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: "Despite ..., still", stressing the contrast and surprise, mostly about others or objective facts; ものの is mostly used for the speaker's own "I did it, but nothing came of it".

similar.title: 〜けれども／〜が
similar.explanation: General contrast or lead-in, the most widely used; ものの only expresses a turn where the facts of the first part don't match the expected outcome.

meaning: A written form for doing two things at once, for contrast (“although ...”), or with 「つつある」 for a change in progress.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + つつ／つつも／つつある

senses.label: While doing
senses.meaning: Two actions at the same time. Same as 「ながら」, but more formal and literary. Both actions must have the same subject.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + つつ
examples: I walked along the mountain path, taking in the beautiful scenery.
I decided on my future path while talking it over with my parents.

senses.label: つつも: although
senses.meaning: Contrast: “even though I knew ..., I still ...”. Often with 「知る」, 「思う」, 「分かる」, or 「言う」, describing doing the opposite of what you know is right.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + つつ(も) (often 「知りつつ」 or 「思いつつ」)
examples: I knew it was wrong, but I lied anyway.
Even though I know it's bad for me, I can't quit smoking.

senses.label: つつある: changing
senses.meaning: A change is steadily moving in one direction and isn't finished yet: “is ...ing”, “is in the process of ...”. Only for verbs of change, not for instantaneous actions.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + つつある (つつあった／つつあります)
examples: The economy is gradually recovering.
Global warming is steadily advancing.

notes: It is mostly found in writing, news, and academic papers. In speech, people say 「ながら」 or 「ている」.
「つつ」 itself doesn't conjugate; 「つつある」 conjugates like 「ある」.

daily.title: Scrolling on your phone late at night
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about a bad habit.
daily.example: I know I should get to bed, but I end up looking at my phone anyway.

daily.title: Closing a letter
daily.description: Ending a letter to a faraway teacher with good wishes.
daily.example: Wishing you good health, I will close here.

work.title: A news report on trends
work.description: News describing an ongoing change.
work.example: More and more companies are introducing remote work.

work.title: Explaining how a project is run
work.description: Describing the approach in a report.
work.example: We are moving the plan forward while incorporating feedback from the field.

etymology: 「つつ」 is a Classical Japanese conjunctive particle already used extensively in Old Japanese texts such as the Man'yōshū, expressing repetition or continuation of an action, or two actions at once. One theory derives it from the reduplication of the perfective auxiliary 「つ」. In waka poetry it often ended a poem to leave a lingering effect (the 「〜つつ」 ending, as in "わが衣手は露にぬれつつ"). The contrastive meaning of 「つつも」 and the progressive meaning of 「つつある」 both developed from the basic sense of "continuing, simultaneous".

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: The most common way to say "while ...ing", used in both speech and writing; つつ is more written and literary. For contrast, 「ながら（も）」 can follow nouns and adjectives (狭いながらも), while 「つつも」 only follows verbs.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Expresses an ongoing action or continuing state; 「つつある」 stresses "in the process of changing in a direction, not yet complete", is more written, and is only used with verbs of change.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Also contrastive, but with ものの the first part is a completed fact; 「つつも」 mostly expresses acting contrary to what one knows or thinks.

meaning: “After / on the basis of ...”, or “in ...ing”, “when it comes to ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form / noun + の + 上で; verb dictionary form + 上で(は／も)

senses.label: After (as a basis)
senses.meaning: Do the first thing, then use its result as a basis for the second: “after ...ing”, “having ...ed”. It stresses that the first part is a necessary step and implies care. The second part is usually an important decision or action.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 上で; noun + の + 上で (相談の上で, 確認の上で)
examples: Please think it over carefully before you decide.
Please sign after checking the contents.
After talking it over with my parents, I decided to study abroad.

senses.label: In ...ing
senses.meaning: “In the process of doing something”, “for the purpose of ...”. The second part is usually an evaluation like 「大切だ」, 「必要だ」, or 「問題」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 上で(は／も)
examples: What's the most important thing in learning a foreign language?
Money is essential for daily life.

senses.label: In terms of
senses.meaning: After a noun, it means looking at something from a certain angle: “in terms of ...”, “on paper”. Often 「〜の上では」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 上では (計算の上では, 法律の上では)
examples: It's possible on paper, but difficult in practice.
Legally, there's no problem.

notes: Before a noun, use 「上での」: 「話し合った上での結論」.
Don't confuse it with the location 「机の上で」 (on the desk). It's also often written in hiragana as 「うえで」.

daily.title: Comparing products before buying online
daily.description: A friend urges you to order, but you want to check reviews first.
daily.example: I'll read the reviews before deciding whether to buy it.

daily.title: Deciding to move with family
daily.description: Explaining to a friend how the decision was made.
daily.example: After talking it over with my family, we decided to move.

work.title: Signing a contract
work.description: Staff ask a customer to check before signing.
work.example: Please review the contract terms before signing.

work.title: Training new employees
work.description: A senior tells newcomers what matters most at work.
work.example: At work, reporting, keeping people informed, and consulting are essential.

etymology: Made of the noun 「上（うえ）」 plus the case particle 「で」. 「上」 originally means "above, on top" in space, and extended to "on top of something = on its basis, after it" and "in terms of ..., in matters of ...". This extension from spatial to abstract meanings (order, field) is seen in Japanese from the Middle Japanese period onward (e.g. 「身の上」, "one's circumstances"). (Compare English "on top of that" and "upon reflection".)

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: Simply expresses time order; た上で stresses that the second action is done "on the basis of the first, after the first has been done thoroughly", implying care.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: Expresses order, "after ...", common in speech; た上で is more written and stresses that the first action is a necessary prerequisite for the second.

similar.title: 〜において
similar.explanation: Expresses a field or occasion, "in ..."; when 「〜上で」 expresses a field it usually pairs with evaluations like "important, necessary, problem", and it can follow the verb dictionary form (生きていく上で).

meaning: From 「限る」 (to limit). It means “as long as ...”, “unless ...”, “as far as ... know”, “as much as possible”, or “limited to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / nai-form + 限り; noun + の／に + 限り

senses.label: As long as
senses.meaning: While the first state lasts, the second stays true. The second part is usually a resolution or judgment.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form + 限り; noun + である + 限り
examples: As long as my stamina holds out, I want to keep running.
As long as I live, I'll never forget you.

senses.label: Unless
senses.meaning: 「〜ない限り」 sets the only condition: unless A happens, B will (or won't) hold true.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + 限り
examples: Unless it rains, the game will go ahead.
I won't forgive him unless he apologizes.

senses.label: As far as ... know
senses.meaning: With verbs like 「知る」, 「聞く」, and 「調べる」, it limits the scope of your information. The tone is cautious.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / ている-form / dictionary form + 限り(では)
examples: As far as I know, he's someone you can trust.
As far as we could find, there were no problems.

senses.label: As much as possible
senses.meaning: Going to the maximum extent. Common in 「できる限り」, 「力の限り」, and 「声の限り」.
senses.connection: できる限り; noun + の + 限り
examples: I'll get back to you as soon as I can.
We fought with everything we had.

senses.label: Limited to
senses.meaning: 「〜に限り」 restricts something to a certain scope. Common in ads and notices.
senses.connection: Noun + に + 限り
examples: Today only, everything is half price.
A gift will be given to the first 100 customers only.

notes: 「限りない」 (limitless) is an adjective, not this grammar point.
Both the kanji 「限り」 and hiragana 「かぎり」 are common.

daily.title: A supermarket sale
daily.description: A supermarket announces today's special.
daily.example: Today only, eggs are half price.

daily.title: Cheering up a friend
daily.description: Encouraging a friend who's worried about an exam.
daily.example: As long as you don't give up, you've got a chance.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: A friend asks what you think of a place.
daily.example: As far as I know, that place is the best.

work.title: Replying to a client email
work.description: Promising a client a quick response.
work.example: We will respond as quickly as possible.

work.title: Explaining meeting arrangements
work.description: Saying the meeting won't change easily.
work.example: Unless something serious comes up, the meeting will go ahead as planned.

etymology: 「限り」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「限る（かぎる）」, originally meaning "boundary, limit, end". Theories differ about the earlier origin of 「限る」, but its core meaning has always been "to set a boundary, to limit". From "boundary" it extended to "within the range of (as long as)", "reaching the limit (doing one's utmost)", and "restricting (only)". Classical Japanese also had 「〜の限り」 meaning "all, every" (e.g. "あるかぎり").

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Uses the same verb 「限る」 but means "not necessarily ...", a partial negation; completely different from 「限り」 (as long as, limited to).

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: "While ...", stressing doing something before the state changes; 限り means "as long as that state continues, the second part holds", stressing the condition rather than the timing.

similar.title: 〜さえ〜ば
similar.explanation: "As long as ...", stressing the sole condition (お金さえあれば); 「〜限り」 focuses more on "for the period this state continues" and carries a tone of determination or assertion.

meaning: “Tend to ...”, “prone to ...” Some (usually bad) tendency often shows up, even if unintended.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) / noun + がち; conjugates like a na-adjective (がちだ／がちな／がちの)

senses.label: Tend to (actions)
senses.meaning: After a verb, it means a behavior often happens, usually a negative one. Often with 「つい」, 「どうしても」, or 「〜と」. Not used for good things (×成功しがち).
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + がちだ／がちになる
examples: In winter, I always seem to catch colds.
When I'm busy, I tend to skip meals.

senses.label: Often in a state
senses.meaning: After a few set nouns, it means often being in a certain state. Common ones: 「病気がち」, 「留守がち」, 「曇りがち」, 「遠慮がち」.
senses.connection: Noun + がち (病気がち, 留守がち, 曇りがち, etc.)
examples: He was often sick as a child and missed a lot of school.
Lately we've had a lot of cloudy weather.

senses.label: ありがち
senses.meaning: 「ありがち」 has become a common word meaning “typical, all too common, cliché”. Before a noun, use 「ありがちな」.
senses.connection: ありがちな + noun; 〜にありがちだ
examples: It's a mistake young people often make.
That's a pretty common story.

notes: Before a noun, both 「がちな」 and 「がちの」 are possible.
It shows a strong tendency or high frequency, not something that always happens.

daily.title: Reflecting on your habits
daily.description: Telling a friend you always procrastinate.
daily.example: When there's a deadline, I tend to keep putting things off.

daily.title: The weather forecast
daily.description: Watching the morning weather on TV.
daily.example: Tomorrow will be mostly cloudy.

daily.title: Noticing the neighbors
daily.description: Mentioning that the neighbors are often away lately.
daily.example: The people next door seem to be away a lot lately.

work.title: Guiding new employees
work.description: A senior warns newcomers about common mistakes.
work.example: New people tend to forget to double-check, so be careful.

etymology: 「がち」 is generally thought to be the voiced form of the noun 「勝ち（かち）」 (winning). 「勝ち」 originally meant "prevailing, having the upper hand", and after other words it meant "a certain element predominates", as in 「黒勝ち」 (mostly black) or 「涙がち」 (often in tears); from this it extended to "... tends to appear, a strong tendency toward ...". The form 「〜がちなり」 is already found in classical texts.

similar.title: 〜やすい
similar.explanation: "Easy to ...", meaning the action itself is easy to do or likely to happen (分かりやすい, 壊れやすい), for good or bad; がち means some undesirable tendency often appears, stressing frequency.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Means "having a feel of ..., prone to ..." (忘れっぽい, 子供っぽい), more colloquial and mostly about personality traits; がち refers more to a temporary tendency and is more written.

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: Means "full of ..., covered in ...", about large quantities spread over a surface; がち expresses tendency or frequency.

meaning: “Covered in ...”, “full of ...” There's too much of something (usually bad), all over the place.
connection: Noun + だらけ; だらけだ／だらけの + noun／だらけになる

senses.label: Covered in (physical)
senses.meaning: A surface is covered in mud, blood, dust, and so on. It gives a dirty, unpleasant feeling.
senses.connection: Noun (泥, 血, 傷, ほこり, ゴミ, etc.) + だらけ
examples: The kids were playing and got covered in mud.
Looking at my grandfather's scarred hands, I thought of all his hardships.
The room is full of trash; there's nowhere to even step.

senses.label: Full of (abstract)
senses.meaning: There's far too much of something abstract, like mistakes, problems, contradictions, or debt. It carries the speaker's dissatisfaction or disgust.
senses.connection: Noun (間違い, 問題, 矛盾, 借金, etc.) + だらけ
examples: This essay is riddled with mistakes.
This plan is full of problems.

notes: It is usually not used for positive things. For neutral or positive “all ...”, use 「〜ずくめ」 or 「〜でいっぱい」.
The verb 「だらける」 (to slack off) is unrelated: 「だらけた生活」.

daily.title: A child back from soccer
daily.description: A mother sees her child come home covered in mud.
daily.example: You're all muddy again!

daily.title: Spring cleaning
daily.description: Opening a storage room that hasn't been used in ages.
daily.example: The storage room was full of dust.

daily.title: Gossiping about someone's debts
daily.description: Talking about someone's finances.
daily.example: I hear he's drowning in debt.

work.title: Checking a junior's report
work.description: A boss criticizes a report after reading it.
work.example: This report is full of mistakes. Go over it again.

etymology: 「だらけ」 is a suffix whose origin is debated, with several theories and no consensus. One theory links it to words like 「だらだら」 and 「だらける」, which express things clinging all over or a loose, slack state; another holds that it is a sound change of an old suffix meaning "full of". It is not normally written with kanji. What is certain is that it gradually spread in colloquial speech from the early modern period onward, meaning "all over, full of".

similar.title: 〜まみれ
similar.explanation: Also means "covered in", but only for liquids, powders, etc. coating a surface (汗まみれ, 泥まみれ, 血まみれ), and can't be used for abstract quantities like "間違いまみれ"; だらけ has a wider range.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: Means "entirely, nothing but" and can be used for good things (いいことずくめ, 黒ずくめの服); だらけ is mostly negative.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: Expresses a tendency, something that often happens; だらけ expresses a large quantity spread all over.

meaning: “Along ...”, or “in line with ...” (a policy or wishes), staying consistent with it.
connection: Noun + に沿って／に沿い; before a noun: noun + に沿った／に沿う + noun

senses.label: Along (physical)
senses.meaning: After long things like rivers, roads, railways, and coastlines, it means extending or moving along them.
senses.connection: 川／道／線路／海岸 + に沿って
examples: A row of cherry trees runs along the river.
We walked along the coast.

senses.label: In line with
senses.meaning: After policies, plans, manuals, requests, or expectations, it means keeping your actions consistent with them: “following ...”, “in line with ...”.
senses.connection: 方針／計画／マニュアル／要望 + に沿って (に沿い／に沿った + noun)
examples: Please carry out the work according to the manual.
We will propose a plan that meets your requirements.
In line with company policy, we introduced a new system.

senses.label: Living up to expectations
senses.meaning: In the set phrase 「ご期待に沿えるよう」, 「沿える」 is the potential form: “so that we can live up to your expectations”.
senses.connection: ご期待／ご希望 + に沿える(よう)
examples: I'll do my very best to live up to your expectations.

notes: 「沿う」 sounds the same as 「添う」. For “to follow, to conform to”, 「沿う」 is the usual modern spelling. It's also often written in hiragana as 「にそって」.

daily.title: Your walking route
daily.description: Describing your weekend route to a friend.
daily.example: On weekends I go jogging along the river.

daily.title: Scenery from the train
daily.description: Introducing a scenic railway line.
daily.example: Rapeseed flowers are blooming along the tracks.

work.title: Making a proposal to a client
work.description: A salesperson presents tailored plans.
work.example: We've prepared several plans that fit your budget.

work.title: Briefing a new hire
work.description: A senior explains that work follows the manual.
work.example: Please follow the manual as you do the work.

etymology: From the verb 「沿う（そう）」, originally meaning "to go along something, to move close beside it". It is generally thought to share its origin with 「添う（そう）」, meaning "to accompany, to be added to". From physically "following along a long object" it extended to the abstract "acting in line with a policy or expectations, staying consistent with them". 「沿って」 is the te-form of 「沿う」 (with a geminate sound change). (Compare English "along the lines of ...".)

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: "Based on ..., on the basis of ...": the first part is the grounds or basis (データ, 法律, 事実), and the second arises from it; に沿って means "following, in line with", keeping actions consistent with a policy or expectations, without stressing "grounds".

similar.title: 〜に従って
similar.explanation: "In accordance with" instructions or rules (指示に従って), with a stronger sense of obedience; it can also mean "as ... (changes)" (年をとるに従って). に沿って focuses more on "not deviating from the direction".

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Expresses means, cause, basis, or "differs depending on ...", with a wide range of uses; に沿って only means "along" or "in line with".

meaning: “Based on ...” Uses the first part as grounds for a judgment, action, or creation.
connection: Noun + に基づいて／に基づき; before a noun: noun + に基づく／に基づいた + noun

senses.label: Based on
senses.meaning: The first part is something that can serve as grounds, such as data, facts, laws, or rules. The second is a judgment or action taken on that basis. It stresses that the basis is legitimate.
senses.connection: Noun + に基づいて／に基づき (written connective)
examples: It's important to make decisions based on data.
Based on the survey results, we drew up a new plan.

senses.label: Based on (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「に基づく」 or 「に基づいた」: “... based on ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に基づく／に基づいた + noun
examples: Please follow the procedures set out by law.
Advice based on experience is really valuable.

senses.label: Based on (works)
senses.meaning: 「〜は…に基づいている」 means a work or system is based on something, like a film based on a true story.
senses.connection: 〜は + noun + に基づいている
examples: This movie is based on a true story.

notes: In kana it's 「もとづく」 (with づ, not ず), because it comes from 「もと＋つく」.
It's common in writing and formal settings. In speech, 「〜をもとに」 is also used.

daily.title: Recommending a movie
daily.description: Recommending a film to a friend.
daily.example: Apparently this movie is based on a true story.

daily.title: A health seminar
daily.description: A doctor introduces dietary advice at a seminar.
daily.example: I'd like to introduce a diet based on the latest research.

work.title: Writing an improvement plan
work.description: Explaining the basis for a plan in a report.
work.example: We created an improvement plan based on the survey results.

work.title: At a government office counter
work.description: Staff explain the basis for the procedure.
work.example: We will proceed with the paperwork in accordance with the regulations.

etymology: 「基づく」 is made of the noun 「基（もと）」 (root, foundation) plus the verb 「付く（つく）」 (to attach), with 「つく」 voiced to 「づく」. Literally "attached to the foundation", it extended to "to be grounded in ...". Precisely because it comes from 「つく」, modern kana spelling rules require 「もとづく」.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: Acting "in line with, following" a policy or expectations, stressing not deviating; に基づいて stresses that the first part is the grounds or basis from which the second is derived or built.

similar.title: 〜をもとに（して）
similar.explanation: "Using ... as material or a basis", mostly for creative work or production (小説をもとに映画を作る), more colloquial; に基づいて stresses the legitimacy of the basis and is more written.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: When it means "according to" (規則によって) it is close to に基づいて, but によって also has many other uses: cause, means, the agent in passives, etc.

meaning: “Not necessarily ...”, “not always ...” Points out exceptions to something people take for granted (a partial denial).
connection: Plain form (だ after nouns / na-adjectives can be dropped) + とは限らない

senses.label: Not necessarily
senses.meaning: Raises an exception to the idea that “it's generally like this”. Often with 「必ずしも」, 「いつも」, or 「〜からといって」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは限らない (often with 「必ずしも」 or 「〜からといって」)
examples: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
Just because someone is Japanese doesn't mean they like sushi.
The forecast isn't always right, so let's take an umbrella.

senses.label: Might well
senses.meaning: 「〜ないとも限らない」 is a double negative: “you can't rule out that ...”. There is some possibility, usually of something bad.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + とも限らない
examples: If you let your guard down, an accident could happen.
Someone might see us.

notes: The polite form is 「とは限りません」; the written connective is 「とは限らず」.
Compared with 「わけではない」, it points out more clearly that exceptions exist.

daily.title: Challenging a stereotype
daily.description: A friend says heavy people all love sweets, and you push back.
daily.example: Not everyone who's overweight likes sweets, you know.

daily.title: Taking an umbrella anyway
daily.description: Family says it'll be sunny, but you take an umbrella.
daily.example: Even if they forecast sun, you can't be sure it won't rain.

work.title: Evaluating applicants

work.example: A strong academic background doesn't necessarily mean someone is good at the job.

work.title: A reminder to back up data
work.description: The IT department reminds everyone to back up regularly.

etymology: Made of the quotative particle 「と」 + the topic particle 「は」 + 「限らない」, the negative of the verb 「限る」. 「限る」 means "to limit, to be restricted to", so 「〜とは限らない」 literally means "it is not limited to the case of ...", i.e. "there are other cases, not necessarily". 「は」 serves to contrast and limit the scope of the negation, producing a partial negation.

similar.title: 〜限り
similar.explanation: Uses the same verb 「限る」, but 「限り」 means "as long as ..., limited to ..., to the utmost ...", completely different from the partial negation "not necessarily".

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Also a partial negation, "it's not that ...", focusing on denying an inference the listener might draw (嫌いなわけではない); とは限らない focuses on pointing out that "exceptions exist" and often pairs with 「必ずしも」.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Expresses possibility, "maybe"; 「〜ないとも限らない」 also expresses possibility but in a more pessimistic tone, stressing "it can't be ruled out".

meaning: “Not only ... but (even) ...” Beyond the first point, there's something that goes further. Often carries surprise.
connection: Noun + ばかりか; verb / i-adjective plain form + ばかりか; na-adjective stem + な + ばかりか

senses.label: Not only ... but also (good)
senses.meaning: The first point is already good, and the second goes further. The second part often has 「も」 or 「まで」, showing admiration.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + ばかりか、〜も
examples: This place isn't just cheap, the food is good too.
She speaks not only English but French as well.

senses.label: Not only ... but even (bad)
senses.meaning: Things keep getting worse, and the second part is even more extreme. Often with 「まで」 or 「さえ」, showing surprise or dissatisfaction.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + ばかりか、〜まで／さえ
examples: Not only does he not do his homework, he sleeps in class.
Not only is it raining, but the wind has picked up too.

notes: The second part can't be a command, request, or intention. Use 「だけでなく」 for that.
In speech, 「ばっかりか」 is also used.
「〜たばかりかもしれない」 is 「ばかり」 + 「かもしれない」, not this grammar point.

etymology: Made of the adverbial particle 「ばかり」 plus the particle 「か」. 「ばかり」 is generally thought to come from 「はかり」, the continuative form of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning "about, approximately" (an estimate), later developing the limiting sense "only, just". 「か」 was originally a particle of questions and rhetorical questions, so 「〜ばかりか」 literally means something like "is it only ...?", and from this rhetorical question came the additive meaning "not only ... (but something more)".

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, "not only ... but also", but plainer in tone; ばかりか puts more stress on the surprising degree of the second part. Neither is commonly used with commands or requests.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: The most common "not only ... but also", used in speech and writing; the second part can be a command, request, or intention. ばかりか is more written and exclamatory.

similar.title: 〜どころか
similar.explanation: "Far from ..., on the contrary / even ...", often rejecting the first part and presenting an opposite or extreme fact (儲かるどころか損をした); ばかりか accepts the first part and adds to it.
